Emerging Church
ee-MER-jing CHURCH
noun phrase (movement)
Late-1990s and early-2000s American Christian movement loosely associated with the Emergent Village network (Brian McLaren, Doug Pagitt, Tony Jones), proposing a postmodern reframing of evangelical Christianity for the "emerging" postmodern generation. Distinct from but overlapping with the related "emergent church" (q.v.) label.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Emerging Church was a late-1990s through early-2010s American Christian movement that proposed a postmodern reframing of evangelical Christianity for what its leaders called the "emerging" postmodern cultural generation. Major representatives: Brian McLaren (A New Kind of Christian, 2001; A Generous Orthodoxy, 2004; A New Kind of Christianity, 2010); Doug Pagitt (Solomon's Porch, Minneapolis); Tony Jones (Emergent Village); Rob Bell (Mars Hill Bible Church, Grand Rapids; Love Wins, 2011). Key features: skepticism toward propositional doctrine and systematic theology; preference for narrative theology and story-based preaching; suspicion of evangelical certainty as a remnant of modernism; openness to postmodern epistemology and to ecumenical-Roman-Catholic-Orthodox sources; gradual softening on biblical sexuality, eschatology, atonement theory, and (in Bell's case) the doctrine of hell. The movement reached its public peak around 2005-2010 and effectively dissolved or transformed by 2015 into either (a) full progressive Christianity (McLaren, Pagitt; the Wild Goose Festival orbit) or (b) the broader exvangelical / deconstruction movement (Bell, Rachel Held Evans). The Reformed-confessional engagement: the Emerging Church's epistemological-postmodern reframing of biblical authority was rebutted in real time by D.A. Carson (Becoming Conversant with the Emerging Church, 2005), Mark Driscoll's harder break, and Kevin DeYoung & Ted Kluck (Why We're Not Emergent, 2008). The dictionary names the movement as the late-1990s-through-2010s evangelical-adjacent transition into what became progressive Christianity.

EMERGING CHURCH, noun phrase. Late-1990s through early-2010s American Christian movement.

Major representatives: Brian McLaren; Doug Pagitt; Tony Jones; Rob Bell; the Emergent Village network.

Key features: skepticism toward propositional doctrine; narrative theology preference; suspicion of evangelical certainty as modernist remnant; postmodern epistemology; ecumenical openness; gradual softening on biblical sexuality, hell, atonement theory.

Peak: 2005-2010; effective dissolution by 2015 into progressive Christianity (McLaren, Pagitt) or the exvangelical / deconstruction movement (Bell, Rachel Held Evans).

Reformed-confessional rebuttals in real time: D.A. Carson (Becoming Conversant with the Emerging Church, 2005); Mark Driscoll (harder break); Kevin DeYoung & Ted Kluck (Why We're Not Emergent, 2008).

📖 Key Scripture

2 Timothy 4:3-4 — "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables."

Galatians 1:6-9 — "I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel: Which is not another; but there are some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ."

Jude 1:3 — "Beloved... it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

1 Timothy 6:20-21 — "O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called: Which some professing have erred concerning the faith."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Emerging Church is itself a corruption pattern being named: the late-1990s-through-2010s evangelical-adjacent transition that softened propositional doctrine, biblical authority, and historic Christian eschatology in the name of postmodern engagement, and that effectively dissolved into progressive Christianity or the deconstruction movement.

expand to see more

Postmodern epistemology as biblical authority-softener. The Emerging Church's central move was epistemological: treating evangelical certainty about biblical authority, propositional doctrine, and systematic theology as a remnant of modernist Enlightenment confidence that the postmodern generation could no longer share. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: biblical authority is not derived from modernist epistemological confidence; it derives from God's self-revelation in inspired Scripture (2 Tim 3:16). The postmodern question ("can you really know?") is the same question the serpent asked in Eden ("Yea, hath God said?" Gen 3:1). The Reformed-confessional answer is the same as the apostolic answer: yes, God has spoken; the prophetic Word is more sure (2 Pet 1:19); the faith was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3).

Trajectory from softening to dissolution. The Emerging Church's leaders did not stop at the postmodern epistemological move; they progressively softened on biblical sexuality (McLaren, Bell, eventually all major figures), on the doctrine of hell (Bell's Love Wins, 2011), on substitutionary penal atonement (McLaren's A New Kind of Christianity, 2010), and ultimately on the gospel itself. By 2015 the movement had effectively dissolved into either full progressive Christianity or the broader exvangelical / deconstruction movement. The trajectory confirms what the Reformed-confessional critics warned in real time: the postmodern epistemological softening was not stable; once the "you can't really know" move was granted, the doctrinal substance progressively eroded along predictable lines. The dictionary names this trajectory plainly.
